title: Victory and Catastrophe
subtitle: The front and the first day of the Babyn Yar massacre
author: R.G. Cruise
phase: III — The Battle for Strategic Objectives
summary: German formations regrouped for further operations as the Moscow supply conference opened and the mass murder at Babyn Yar began. The military assessment and the history of occupation reveal connected consequences of the same invasion.
body:
Two consequences of conquest

On 29 September 1941, the German victory around Kiev was being converted into preparations for another offensive. Formations that had fought southward were regrouping, supply organisations were trying to support new concentrations, and the German high command again expected a major operation in the centre to bring a decision. In occupied Kiev, meanwhile, Jewish families were moving toward an assembly point under an order backed by the threat of death. Their destination was the killing ground at Babyn Yar. These events belonged to the same invasion, but they require different kinds of explanation: one concerns the continuing struggle between armies, the other the deliberate murder of people placed under German power.[1][2]

The five weeks covered by this phase had transformed the military situation. Leningrad’s principal land connection with the Soviet interior had been severed; the German salient at Yelnya had been evacuated under Soviet pressure; and the Southwestern Front had suffered a catastrophic encirclement. None of those outcomes can simply stand for the entire campaign. Germany had won an enormous battle in the south without defeating the Soviet Union. The Red Army had achieved a local success in the centre without removing the danger to Moscow. Leningrad remained Soviet, but its survival now depended on a supply problem of exceptional severity.[3]

A final assessment must therefore hold military capacity and human consequences together. The familiar question of whether Germany should have driven directly on Moscow cannot encompass what the campaign had done to the people in its path. Nor should the crimes of occupation be treated as events that happened after the fighting had become historically important. Military conquest supplied the territory, coercive power and institutional access through which those crimes could be organised. The army’s continuing operational problems did not prevent German authorities from devoting personnel and administrative effort to mass murder.

The northern objective remains beyond reach

By the end of September, Army Group North had isolated Leningrad from its main overland supply routes without capturing the city. The loss of Shlisselburg on 8 September remained decisive because it closed the connection along the southern side of Lake Ladoga. The Soviet position still included access to the lake, but access alone could not feed a metropolis and its defending armies. Cargo required a route to the eastern shore, vessels and loading facilities for the crossing, and transport onward from the western shore. Each stage imposed a separate limit on what could actually reach the people who needed it.[3][4]

The distinction between geographical opening and effective capacity, developed in Leningrad Cut Off, had become more urgent rather than less. A cargo waiting at a distant railhead was not available to a bakery inside the city. A successful voyage did not guarantee a dependable daily volume. Loading, unloading, onward distribution and the return of vessels all had to continue under wartime conditions. The lake connection preserved possibilities, but it did not justify describing the city as adequately supplied. Its existence and its insufficiency could both be true.

Finnish forces formed another part of the northern situation. Their positions across the Karelian Isthmus and along the Svir east of Ladoga constrained Soviet options, while Finnish political objectives and command decisions remained distinct from those of the German army group. The U.S. Army synthesis of the late-September front places the Finnish line on the Svir alongside the German position at Shlisselburg. The two should not be joined on a map as though the whole intervening territory had been occupied or the lake enclosed by a continuous land front. The remaining geography was central to Soviet survival.[3]

German policy had also become explicit. The directive of 22 September, later introduced at Nuremberg as document C-124, envisaged enclosing and destroying Leningrad while refusing responsibility for feeding its population, even in the event of surrender. By 29 September, the instruction formed part of the documented German policy governing the treatment of a city whose supply connections had already been gravely restricted. It turns the supply crisis into more than an accidental consequence of interrupted communications. German leaders intended to exploit the population’s vulnerability. The subsequent winter catastrophe still lay ahead, but the policy that made civilian starvation an instrument of conquest was already present.[5]

At the same time, the transfer of mobile forces toward Army Group Centre constrained what the northern command could attempt next. The choice to concentrate for Moscow did not eliminate Leningrad as an objective; it changed the balance between assault, containment and future operations around the lake. Resources committed to one strategic aim were unavailable elsewhere. This continuing redistribution is a better explanation of the front’s development than the assumption that every German army group advanced with a permanently adequate and independent allocation of strength.[3]

Yelnya, Kiev and the unfinished southern campaign

In the centre, the Soviet recapture of Yelnya in early September had removed a German salient and demonstrated that sustained attacks could compel a withdrawal. It had not destroyed Army Group Centre or secured the approaches to Moscow. The German command was now bringing mobile formations back into that theatre and reinforcing them from elsewhere. The experience at Yelnya therefore belonged to a continuing contest in which local success and strategic danger coexisted. Its defenders and attackers had learned something about the cost of concentrated fighting; neither side had been released from the consequences of losses already incurred.[3]

The victory around Kiev altered the southern balance more radically. Much of the Southwestern Front had ceased to exist as an organised force, and German armies could prepare to move toward new objectives beyond the Dnieper. Yet the end of the pocket battle did not make the whole southern theatre available for unrestricted exploitation. The U.S. Army campaign study describes continued operations toward Kharkov and the southern approaches while forces were also required at the entrance to the Crimea. Movement to those objectives depended upon the condition of the formations emerging from the previous operation and upon the supply routes behind them.[1]

Odessa remained in Soviet hands on 29 September. The Romanian forces besieging it had not obtained the rapid result that a general map of German progress across Ukraine might suggest, and German assistance was required. This was an important qualification to any claim that the southern campaign had been completed. A defended coastal city could continue to demand troops and attention after the main front had moved far beyond its latitude. Its maritime setting also made its military problem different from that of the landlocked Kiev pocket. Encirclement on land did not automatically create the same conditions everywhere.[1]

The Crimea presented another geographical obstacle. The German attempt to force the Perekop Isthmus on 26 September confronted a narrow entrance in which defenders could concentrate their resistance. The wide operational movements that had brought success around Kiev could not simply be repeated across the same kind of frontage. The German 11th Army under Erich von Manstein faced a distinct task, while Soviet forces elsewhere in the southern theatre continued to threaten German and allied dispositions. Capturing territory had multiplied Germany’s commitments as well as creating opportunities.[1][3]

These differences explain why the phase ends with an assessment rather than a single verdict on momentum. German operational success was real, Soviet losses were severe, and further German advances remained possible. The defending state nevertheless retained armies outside the destroyed pocket, an industrial system being reorganised and the ability to create new formations. The important question was how quickly those resources could become effective military power. Possessing manpower somewhere in the Soviet Union did not mean that trained, equipped troops were already available at the threatened point.

The material condition of another offensive

German planners faced the corresponding problem of converting nominal resources into an effective concentration. The campaign study compiled for the U.S. Army records 409,998 personnel losses in the Russian theatre between 22 June and 31 August, against 217,000 replacements that had actually arrived by the latter date. These are theatre-wide figures for that defined period, not casualties in the Kiev battle alone. Their significance is the gap between losses and delivered replacements before September’s fighting had run its course. Men allocated on paper or expected later could not fill the places of those already absent.[1]

Equipment presented an additional constraint. Tanks undergoing repair, trucks awaiting parts and transport worn by repeated long movements limited what formations could do after they were reassigned. Reorientation required more than a new arrow on a headquarters map. Workshops and supply columns had to find their units, roads had to carry movement in the required direction, and the rail system had to deliver fuel and ammunition to usable unloading points. The forces gathering for another offensive were the products of the summer’s campaigning, with its accumulated wear and uneven replenishment.[1]

Guderian’s retrospective account describes a particularly revealing difficulty in preparing the next attack: supplies and replacements intended for his group were still being sent toward Orsha, associated with its earlier position, while it needed them farther south. His precise estimates should be read as a participant’s later account, but the underlying problem is concrete. An army could have supplies allocated to it and still lack them where the next operation required them. Previous movements left an administrative trail that had to be corrected as well as a physical distance that had to be covered.[6]

This evidence also limits the familiar counterfactual about an earlier advance on Moscow. A direct offensive in August would have required assumptions about Soviet resistance, flank security, available vehicles and supply capacity. It cannot be evaluated merely by transferring the days spent in the south to an imagined uninterrupted movement eastward. The choice of objectives mattered, but so did the forces and communications available to pursue them. By late September, the actual German decision was to attempt another major concentration despite the material difficulties that its own records and later studies describe.

Moscow negotiates for the means to continue

On the Soviet side, international assistance was becoming a practical military question. The first formal meeting of the British, American and Soviet delegations in Moscow was scheduled for 29 September. W. Averell Harriman and Lord Beaverbrook had met Stalin and Molotov at the Kremlin the previous evening. The timing matters: while Germany was preparing to exploit its victory, the Soviet leadership was negotiating for resources with which to continue the war. These negotiations did not restore the armies lost at Kiev, but they demonstrate that the political and material struggle extended beyond the immediate battlefield.[7]

The ambassadors leave the room

American ambassador Laurence Steinhardt recorded a small but revealing incident at the opening of the Moscow discussions. Before the meeting on 28 September, Beaverbrook asked that British ambassador Stafford Cripps withdraw after the introductions. Steinhardt and Cripps then both left. Harriman later told Steinhardt that he understood Beaverbrook’s purpose as an attempt to overcome the lack of confidence that had developed between London and Moscow. The episode belongs to a contemporary diplomatic report, although Harriman’s explanation remained his interpretation of Beaverbrook’s motive. It shows negotiations beginning with decisions about people and relationships as well as lists of equipment. A supply agreement required confidence that promises would be honoured, but the participants did not arrive with equal trust in one another. The departure of two ambassadors briefly exposed the work involved in constructing a coalition whose military need was already urgent.[7]

The discussions quickly became specific. In a telegram sent on 30 September, Harriman reported Stalin’s interest in light tanks carrying cannon and adequate armour, together with a particularly strong demand for antitank and antiaircraft guns. He also reported Stalin’s belief that German tank strength greatly exceeded Soviet strength. That statement records the Soviet leader’s assessment during negotiations; it is not an independently verified ratio of serviceable vehicles. The distinction preserves what the document actually tells us: the leadership’s perception of its material weakness and the categories of assistance it considered urgent.[8]

The agreement reached immediately afterward also exposed the distance between commitment and delivery. Reporting the conclusion on 1 October, Harriman stated that the American side would make the authorized supplies available, but that it had made no commitment on transportation, offering assistance instead. That qualification is central to the military history. Equipment had to be manufactured or released, moved to a port, carried through dangerous routes and distributed within the Soviet Union before a front could use it. Diplomacy could establish entitlement to supplies without solving every stage of their journey.[9]

For Poland’s government in exile, the same negotiations raised questions that reached back to the events covered in the atlas’s first collection. On 8 September, the Polish ambassador in Washington had requested Polish representation, arguing that discussions with the Soviet Union could affect vital Polish interests and that Polish forces being organised in Soviet territory needed equipment. The American response emphasised the mission’s immediate military purpose and declined to enlarge its membership. Coalition building therefore did not erase the consequences of the Soviet invasion of Poland or settle the political future of the territories involved. Those disagreements continued within a common struggle against Germany.[10]

The occupation authorities organise murder

In Kiev, the German authorities were using their newly established control for a different purpose. The explosions and fires that began on 24 September, resulting from explosives left by Soviet forces, supplied a pretext for an attack on the city’s Jews. They did not establish collective Jewish responsibility. The decision to target an entire population, including children and elderly people, belonged to the occupiers. Describing the killings as a reprisal without that distinction would reproduce the perpetrators’ justification and obscure the nature of the crime.[11]

The perpetrators’ own records establish that the killing apparatus had arrived with the conquest. Operational Situation Report 106, dated 7 October, recorded an advance party of Sonderkommando 4a entering Kiev with the fighting troops on 19 September, followed by the main detachment on 25 September. Paul Blobel commanded the unit within Einsatzgruppe C. The record places its work beside that of the military authorities securing the city and dealing with demolitions. The machinery of persecution was therefore being established during the occupation’s first days, before the later report claimed that mass murder answered popular anger over the fires.[2]

Historian Kai Struve’s biographical study of Friedrich Jeckeln identifies the cooperation among Jeckeln, Einsatzgruppe C commander Otto Rasch and Kiev’s Wehrmacht commandant, Kurt Eberhard. Jeckeln, as Higher SS and Police Leader, connected the regional police apparatus with the killing units. Blobel’s Sonderkommando supplied a principal executing formation. This was an operation involving identifiable organisations and commanders, rather than an unexplained eruption of violence after a battle. The German Historical Museum also records discussions involving military officers, security police and Einsatzgruppe personnel before the massacre.[12][13]

The official report is explicit about institutional cooperation. It says the assembly order was arranged with the city commandant and posted by members of the newly organised Ukrainian militia. It credits Sonderkommando 4a, the Einsatzgruppe staff and two detachments of Police Regiment South with the killings, and reports military approval. These admissions are sufficient to reject a picture of an army conducting an entirely separate conventional war while an unrelated organisation murdered civilians behind it. They do not establish identical conduct by every soldier; they establish cooperation by institutions whose functions made the operation possible.[2]

The same record must be read critically when it describes the population. Its claims of general approval and its allegations about Jewish conduct served the killers’ explanation of their own actions. They cannot be treated as a representative survey of Kiev or as proof of the accusations. Local collaboration was real and requires examination, but collective guilt cannot be assigned to Ukrainians any more than Nazi accusations can establish collective guilt among Jews. Responsibility follows documented actions, positions and orders. The surviving record identifies German direction and auxiliary participation without making every resident an interchangeable participant.

The road to Babyn Yar

The order posted on 28 September required the Jews of Kiev and the surrounding area to assemble the next morning, bringing documents, valuables and clothing. Failure to appear was punishable by death.[14] Its demands made the rumour of removal plausible: possessions suitable for travel were requested, and the instruction presented obedience as the only lawful course. The threat and the deception worked together. People were being compelled to enter a system whose purpose was concealed from them, under conditions in which refusing the order also appeared lethal.[13][2]

The movement toward the ravine brought households rather than merely isolated individuals into German control. Elderly people needed assistance; children depended on adults; relatives who might have attempted to hide alone could be unwilling to abandon someone else. Such obligations help explain the procession without imagining that the victims possessed either full information or unrestricted choices. An order directed against an entire community placed the ordinary responsibilities of family life inside the machinery of coercion. The belongings carried for supposed resettlement would subsequently become property seized by the killers.

Dina Pronicheva accompanies her family

In a conversation recorded by Soviet historians on 24 April 1946, Dina Pronicheva explained why she joined the movement on 29 September. Her younger sister had remained with sick and elderly relatives, who asked her to accompany them because they expected deportation. Pronicheva left her children with her husband and went with the family. She described barriers near the cemetery through which people could enter but could not freely leave, followed by the confiscation of belongings and separation in the crowd. Later taken to the killing place herself, she survived by falling among the bodies and remaining motionless before struggling out. Her account was retrospective testimony, not a diary written that day. It gives the crime a personal sequence: family assistance became entrapment, and entrapment became an attempt to survive. Her survival preserves a witness to people whose own accounts could never be recorded.[14]

At the ravine, victims were forced to surrender clothing and enter the killing area in groups. German shooters murdered them at close range. The operation continued on 30 September, and the German report stated that 33,771 Jews had been killed across the two days together. That figure is the perpetrators’ reported total for 29–30 September. It is neither a count for the first day alone nor the total number of people murdered at Babyn Yar throughout the occupation. Preserving those distinctions is necessary to understand both the scale of this particular massacre and the later use of the site.[11][2]

The possessions and the report

The German report described the collection of money, valuables, clothing and linen after the murder. Some goods were allocated through the Nazi welfare organisation for ethnic Germans, while others went to the city administration for distribution. Elsewhere the same report presented the apartments of murdered Jews as newly available housing for people displaced by the fires. The victims’ removal was thus translated into administrative benefits for others. Property transfer was not an incidental detail attached to the crime; it was one of the ways in which the occupation absorbed and normalized its consequences.[2]

This language also reveals the distortion produced by reading an administrative report only for its facts and figures. The document described the operation as proceeding without serious difficulty and claimed that knowledge of the actual killings remained limited. Such formulations measured success from the perpetrators’ perspective. They omitted the suffering that made the operation possible only through extreme coercion. The historian’s task is to retain the evidentiary value of the report while refusing its moral vocabulary: the seizure of possessions followed murder, and the supposed availability of apartments meant that their inhabitants had been killed.

The numbers require similar discipline. An exact figure in a report demonstrates the number the organisation transmitted, not the existence of an independently verified individual register available to us. Other parts of the same report used approximate totals when discussing housing. This does not diminish the established reality of the massacre. It shows that different administrative passages could express the same crime with different degrees of numerical precision. Survivor testimony, documentary admissions and the wider historical investigation establish the event through converging evidence; no single numeral carries that burden alone.[2]

The killings also changed the city that remained. Homes, workplaces and family networks lost the people who had sustained them. Some residents participated in the occupation’s institutions or benefited from stolen property; others attempted to assist those in danger. A city cannot be reduced to either response. What German authority had imposed was a system in which Jewish identity itself made a person a target and in which survival depended upon evasion, concealment and help under conditions set by the persecutors. Military victory had created the space for that system, and cooperation among German institutions made it work.

The position reached

By 29 September, Germany could point to major territorial gains and the destruction of Soviet armies, but the strategic objectives that had shaped the invasion remained incompletely achieved. Leningrad had not fallen, Moscow remained beyond the German front, Odessa still resisted, and the Soviet government was assembling new military and international resources. German forces retained the capacity to inflict further disasters, yet their own losses and transport problems imposed limits that could not be removed by another declaration of confidence. The next offensive would begin with those contradictions already present.

Guderian’s attack began on 30 September, opening the next stage of operations toward Moscow. On that same day, the killings at Babyn Yar continued. The offensive and the killings belonged to different chains of action within the same invading power. Their simultaneity shows why the campaign’s military achievements must be examined alongside the institutions and decisions through which conquest exposed civilians to deliberate murder. This phase therefore closes with two conclusions supported by different but connected evidence: the German army had won a great battle without winning the war, and German conquest had exposed civilians to a catastrophe that military totals alone cannot describe.[1][2]

sourceMethod: Numbered citations lead to the sources below; each entry lists the passages cited and links back to its first use. Contemporary orders establish intentions, while reports contain the information, estimates and gaps known to their authors. Retrospective military accounts and testimony are identified and assessed alongside documentary evidence and scholarship. English paraphrases of Russian, Ukrainian and German texts are by the atlas unless a published translator is named. Archival references reproduced in published sources do not imply direct archival inspection. Events after the chapter date are dated explicitly. The companion map is a dated regional military reconstruction; its feature sources and precision notes distinguish reported positions from approximate connecting edges.
